Children and adults in the Netherlands were recruited online (via social media) and through the Leiden University participant recruitment database. Both children and adults in the Netherlands were tested in the labs at Leiden University. In Japan, adults were recruited via a local participant database and tested at Tokyo Woman's Christian University. Children in Japan were recruited and tested as part of a research visit to Miraikan (The National Museum of Emerging Science and Innovation) in addition to laboratory visits at Tokyo Woman's Christian University and Ritsumeikan University in Osaka. Participants were reimbursed according to the standard rates of each local site. In the Netherlands, children received a small toy and a "Young Scientists" certificate as a reward for their participation, while adults received (€7,50) or research credits. The parents of Japanese children received a payment of 6000¥ and Japanese adults received 2500¥, in gift card or cash, in line with local standards.

Participant Exclusions

We had complete self-report data for all participants (except n = 1 Japanese adult), however, due to video processing issues, as well as some participants who obscured their face during the viewing of the stimuli, there were some missing data for the facial expression portion of the analysis. In Japan, n = 5 adults and in the Netherlands n = 1 child and n = 1 adult were missing from the analysis with facial emotional expressions.

Sampling Plan

We used PANGEA (Westfall, 2015), a power analysis tool for general ANOVA designs, to determine our sample size. We performed this power calculation based on a mixed model, which included a random intercept per participant. Country, age, and emotion category were entered as fixed factors. Participants were nested within country and age factors. We powered the study to detect the predicted country x age interaction in emotion intensity. Because distinguishing between the two competing predicted patterns also requires examining country differences within each age category, we ensured that the planned sample size provided sufficient precision for these follow-up simple-effects comparisons. Few studies have directly compared emotion production intensity differences between cultural groups, so we decided to estimate our effect size conservatively, grounded on what we would consider a meaningful effect size of interest. Based on our calculations, a sample size of n = 70 (n = 35 children, n = 35 adults) participants at each site (total N = 140) were needed for 95% power to detect a country × age group interaction effect on emotional expression intensity with a small-to-medium effect size (d = 0.4) at the standard error probability of alpha = .05.

Design

The present study had a factorial design with two between-subjects' factors: age of the expresser (2 levels: adults, children) and country of the expresser (2 levels: Netherlands, Japan) and one within-subjects' factor (which as only of exploratory interest): target emotion of the stimulus (4 levels: happiness, sadness, disgust and fear). As indicated, we examined whether emotional facial expression intensity across different distinct emotions differed across both cultural and age groups.

Procedure

In this study, we performed an emotion-induction task using video stimuli designed to elicit specific emotions across different cultural contexts. This technique has been used in previous studies with children (Khan et al., 2019) and adults (Schaefer et al., 2010). Although participants were made aware that they would be asked to view emotional stimuli, we kept the explicit aims of the study vague and did not divulge which specific emotions we were intending to elicit until the debriefing.

After signing the consent forms, participants were invited to sit in front of a computer screen and fill in some demographic information. Participants were asked to tie their hair back and remove any clothing items that obscured their face. For adult participants, we asked for their: age, gender, country of birth, cultural background (in the Netherlands:

Western/Non-Western/Other/Prefer Not to Say; in Japan: Japanese/Non-Japanese) household income, and highest level of education. For child participants, we asked their parents for their child's: age, gender, country of birth. Additionally, we asked parents to report their own highest level of education, cultural background and household income in the same way as adult participants. For participants not born in the Netherlands or Japan, we asked how long they have lived in the Netherlands or Japan (to control for this if necessary). Both age groups were given written instructions for task, in which the various scales were explained. For children specifically, the researcher read the instructions verbally seated next to the child, so the child had the opportunity to ask for clarification. During the instruction round, participants were shown how the scales work and it was emphasized that more than one emotion category could be chosen (i.e., that it was possible to experience mixed emotions).

For children, the definition of each of the emotion terms was explained to ensure they understood their meaning. The researcher also practiced sliding the scales with the child.

After the instructions, the emotion induction task begun. The researcher (and, in the case of children, the parent) were asked to leave the room. After this, a series of ten short (max 4-minute) video clips, drawn from a series of movies and YouTube videos, were displayed in randomized order. We use different stimuli for children and adults to ensure that the stimuli were age appropriate. These stimuli were drawn from various databases and have been used in previous works to induce happiness, sadness, disgust, fear and neutrality (Gross & Levenson, 1995; Khan et al., 2019; Sato et al., 2007; Schaefer et al., 2010; Zupan & Eskritt, 2020). To maximize the chances of inducing emotions, each participant viewed two videos intended to induce each of the four emotion categories (plus two neutral stimuli). For a full list of stimuli see Supplementary Materials 1. After the participant viewed each video, they were asked to indicate how they felt during the viewing by indicating their emotional state on a sliding scale with a list of emotion words in their native language (e.g., "During this video, I felt happy/sad/disgust/fear/neutral [0-100]") (see Supplementary Materials 1 for translations into Dutch and Japanese). After viewing all the stimuli, the participant was asked to provide permission for their video stimuli to be used in the follow-up emotion recognition project and the experiment was concluded.

Materials

We used a Logitech C920 HD webcam and ring lamp to record individuals during the viewing of the induction videos. We filmed each participant's face and upper body as they sat in front of the screen and watch each video. Participants wore a white t-shirt to keep the recordings as standardized as possible. The webcam was placed on the monitor, at approximately 30cm distance from the participant. Stimuli were displayed and self-report ratings collected using a survey displayed with Qualtrics on a web browser. Videos were derived from popular movies and YouTube clips, ranging from approximately 30 seconds to 4 minutes. We displayed all stimuli to adults with subtitles, and audio dubbing for children (since many of the youngest children were still learning to read).

Video Trimming

Since the induction stimuli used in this study varied in length, and most emotions were likely to occur only at specific points throughout the displayed stimulus material, we trimmed the webcam recordings of participants at pre-specified times such that they were all the same length (20 seconds -see Stimulus List in Supplementary Materials 1). To standardize the stimuli and maximize the chance of these trimmed videos containing facial expressions of emotion but limiting researcher degrees of freedom by manually selecting a unique expression apex for each participant, we pre-specified the to-be-trimmed time portions of each expresser's reaction video. These trim points are indicated in Supplementary Materials 1 and represent 5-seconds before and 15-seconds after the point in the induction video that was most intense and, therefore, likely to be maximally emotion-evoking. For example, we showed an excerpt from the film Forrest Gump to adults to induce happiness, and we trimmed each of the reaction videos to cover the moments before and after the scene in the clip in which the protagonist is reunited with his lover. In this way, each participant's reaction reflected the same moment in the induction stimulus, allowing us to make standardized comparisons across stimuli and participants.

Statistical Analyses

Manipulation Check

To check whether the induction videos induced the intended target emotions, we examined participants' self-report scores on each of the induction videos to determine whether the participants reported feeling the intended target emotion. As per our preregistration, a video was considered "successful" in inducing the target emotion if participants reported, at a group level, significantly higher scores on the target emotion compared to neutral. For example, if the video was intended to induce feelings of happiness, the induction was considered successful if participants reported feeling significantly more happiness than neutral. Since we used different stimuli for children and adults, we used separate models for each age group and collapsed scores across cultures.

Induction success for each age group was tested using a Gaussian linear mixed model using the glmmTMB package (Brooks et al., 2017 ) in R Studio (Citing RStudio, 2023). Here, we used the difference between participants' self-report scores on the target emotion and their scores on neutral as the dependent variable, and video type as a factor (eight levels: corresponding to each of the two videos for each of the four target emotions).

We allowed intercepts to vary across participants. Since we used sum coding for the video type factor, a significant positive intercept would be indicative of a grand mean significantly greater than zero. To examine whether the means were significantly above zero across videos, we inspected the marginal means of the model output to ascertain whether the estimated mean was positive and its 95% CI did not span zero, using the emmeans package (Lenth et al., 2019). This would suggest that the stimulus induced the target emotion to a significantly greater extent than it induced neutrality.

Deriving the Facial Expression Intensity Scores.

After checking the manipulation success of the task, the next step was to derive the facial expression intensity scores based on observable facial action units (AUs). To do this, we process all the 20-second trimmed recordings through an automatic facial expression recognition software package FaceReader (Noldus, 2014). FaceReader classifies facial expressions on the basis of an artificial neural network, trained on manually coded images based on the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) (Ekman & Friesen, 1978). It classified our four emotions of interest: happiness, sadness, fear and disgust on the basis of the activation of the facial action units associated with each emotion's "prototypical" display (e.g., the emotion sadness is constituted by activation of AUs 1 + 4 + 15, corresponding to a raising of the inner brow, lowering of the brow and down turning of the lip corners). For each frame of the video, the software gives an intensity score for each of the above listed emotions between 0-1 at a 10Hz frame rate. We used FaceReader's general facial expression model for Dutch participants, and the East-Asian model for Japanese participants. For our analyses, we examined the FaceReader intensity scores for the target emotion specifically, extracting its peak intensity (i.e., maximum, or apex) within each 20-second clip.

Because group differences in target-emotion intensity scores could reflect crosscultural variation in the broader configuration of facial action units recruited during emotional expression, rather than differences in the prototypical expression of target emotion alone, we additionally conducted an exploratory control analysis of peak-frame AU profiles.

We pooled the two emotion-eliciting videos and identified the single frame with the highest total activity across 19 FaceReader-derived AUs for each participant separately. Within this peak frame, the 19 AUs were ranked from most to least active. We then summarised, within each group, the percentage of participants for whom each AU appeared among the five most prominent AUs for that emotion. This approach allowed us to characterise the relative configuration of facial activity at participants' peak-expression frames, rather than the absolute intensity or presence of individual AUs and is decribed in detail in Supplementary Materials 2. While this analysis revealed some specific differences -most clearly, a lower relative prominence of AU6 (cheek raiser) and AU12 zygomaticus major in Japanese adults' happiness displays -the broader AU profiles showed substantial overlap between groups and generally good correspondence with the theoretically expected emotion displays (Figure S3).

Together, this pattern indicates that the cross-cultural differences in facial-expression intensity reported above are unlikely to be attributable solely to cultural differences in the broader sets of AUs recruited.

Inferential Analyses

As in the manipulation check, we performed all our analyses using the glmmTMB function. Although we did not pre-register this, we firstly looked at the relationship between age and culture on participants' self-reported emotions. Here, we performed a beta linear mixed model with sum coded age of the expresser (child vs. adult), country of the expresser (Netherlands vs. Japan), as well as their interaction, as predictors of self-reported emotional state, for the target emotion specifically. In these analyses, we opted for a Beta-regression as the scores were proportional (0-100, later converted to 0 > score > 1) as this analysis is highly suited to proportional data (Smithson & Verkuilen, 2006). Since Beta-regressions cannot be used for the analysis of proportions equal to zero or one, we scaled the scores according to the formula (1.1): where N is the sample size (Smithson & Verkuilen, 2006, pp. 55).

As above, we allowed intercepts to vary across participants.

EMOTIONS ACROSS CULTURE AND DEVELOPMENT

Next, as per our pre-registration, we performed an additional beta linear mixed model on FaceReader facial emotion maximum intensity scores, with the same fixed effects structure as above. We included a random intercept per participant and nested this within the factors country and age. For ease of interpretation, we followed up all models using the Type 3 ANOVA function from the car package (Fox et al., 2019) and used the emmeans package (Lenth et al., 2019) to contrast the marginal effects. In text, we report the output of the Type 3

ANOVAs, and the output of the full regression models in the Supplementary Materials 2.

Importantly, for all beta linear mixed models, we took the exponent of the model coefficients to interpret the estimates at the odds ratio level. Additionally, in the case of any nonsignificant findings, we also followed up our frequentist tests with Bayesian analyses using the brms function in R Studio, and used the Bayes factor, using bayesfactor_parameters function in the bayestestR package (Makowski et al., 2019), to quantify evidence for and against the null hypothesis. We specified the same model structure as that specified above, and used weakly informative priors for fixed effects (M = 0, SD = 1) and the intercept (M = 0, SD =1).

Exploratory Analyses

In our exploratory analyses, we were interested in examining patterns of responding across specific emotion categories. First, we examined whether there were any differences in the intensity of participants facial expressions for each emotion category using an additional Beta linear mixed model. Here, we included age group, country, and target emotion as fixed effects, allowing the intercepts to vary per participant. Additionally, we were also interested in exploring the relationship between participants' self-reported emotions and their corresponding facial expressions. Specifically, we aimed to determine whether this relationship varied across emotion categories, age groups, and countries. To examine this, we created a generalized linear mixed model, including a random intercept for each participant and allowing slopes to vary within participants for the effect of self-report scores on the target emotion, for each emotion category. All random effects were specified as uncorrelated for computational efficiency.

Results

Manipulation Check

Firstly, we examined whether the emotion induction task resulted in participants reporting having experienced the target emotion significantly more than the amount that they reported feeling neutral, separately for both children and adults. Full model outputs are available in Supplementary Materials 2. In the model on children's self-report, the intercept, representing the grand mean of all the videos displayed, was positive and significant, β = 28.75, 95% CI = [20.27, 37.22], p < .001 (Table S1). This suggests that the stimuli displayed evoked more emotions than neutrality. When homing in on the specific emotion effects for each video in the child group, the marginal means revealed that all stimuli (except both "Fear" videos) resulted in the induction of the target emotion significantly more than neutral (Table S2). In the model on adult's self-report, the intercept was positive and significant, β = 51.72, 95% CI = [45.03, 58.39], p < .001 (Table S3) and adults, therefore, reported feeling the target emotion significantly more than neutral across all emotion stimuli (Table S4).

As such, it appears that all stimuli, except the fearful videos in childhood, resulted in the induction of the intended target emotions. Although the fear stimuli that we displayed to children did not seem to result in the induction of self-reported fear significantly above neutral, the means were positive (indicating an induction in the correct direction), so we decided to nonetheless still include these data in our eventual models in the interest of parsimony, as well as in line with our pre-registered analysis.

Self-Reported Emotions

EMOTIONS ACROSS CULTURE AND DEVELOPMENT

Next, we examined whether there were significant differences across age and countries on participants' self-report ratings of emotions, within one model. The beta linear mixed model revealed no differences across both countries and age groups on self-reported emotion scores, χ 2 (1) = 0.01, p = .930; χ 2 (1) = 2.01, p = .156, respectively. We followed up this test with a Bayesian beta linear mixed model, retaining the same structure, to assess evidence for the null hypothesis (Table S6).

This revealed anecdotal evidence for a lack of difference in self-report across age, OR = 0.77, 95% CI = [0.53-1.12], BF10 = 0.48; and moderate evidence for a lack of difference across countries on self-reported emotion scores, OR = 1.02, 95% CI = [0.71-1.49], BF10 = 0.19. Ultimately, these analyses suggest that participants of different ages and countries did not report feeling emotions of differing intensities during the presentation of our stimuli overall.

Nonverbal Expression Intensity Across Age and Culture

Following our pre-registration, we then examined whether there were significant differences across both age groups and countries in terms of participants' facial expression intensity on the target emotion. The model, displayed in Table 4, revealed a significant main effect of country, χ 2 (1) = 13.12, p < .001. Examination of the contrasts revealed that the odds of Japanese individuals displaying facial emotions with greater intensity were 0.76 times the odds of individuals in the Netherlands, OR = 0.76, 95% CI = [0.66, 0.88]. In other words, Dutch participants were more likely to express emotions with higher intensity compared to Japanese participants. Additionally, we found a significant main effect of age, χ 2 (1) = 5.46, p = .019; with the odds of an adult displaying a higher intensity facial expression 0.84 times the odds of the child group, OR = 0.84, 95% CI = [0.73, 0.97]. In other words, children were more likely to show higher intensity facial expressions, on average, compared to adults.

Examination of Figure 1 further confirms this pattern: Dutch participants were generally more expressive than Japanese participants, and children were generally more expressive than adults.

In line with our hypotheses, we further zoomed in on the extent to which children and adults of different cultures differed in their emotion intensity scores by examining the marginal means. As pre-registered, it was the between-culture differences within each age group that were of primary importance. Although the interaction between age and country was not significant (Table 4), we proceeded with the planned contrasts to directly test our competing pattern of results. The results revealed a significant difference between Japanese and Dutch adults in terms of facial emotion intensity, OR = 1.41, 95% CI = [1.15, 1.74], p = .001. This suggests that Dutch adults were more expressive than Japanese adults. However, no significant differences could be found between Japanese and Dutch children on facial emotion intensity, OR = 1.22, 95% CI = [1.00, 1.48], p = .053. This was confirmed by examination of the contrasts in a follow-up Bayesian independent samples t-test, which revealed moderate evidence for a lack of a difference between Dutch (M = 0.26, SD = 0.30) and Japanese (M = 0.26, SD = 0.30) children on facial emotion intensity, BF10 = 0.22.

Therefore, the difference in emotional expression intensity between Japan and the Netherlands was mostly driven by the differences between adults, not children. on the density map represent regions where data points are more concentrated. For example, Japanese Adults show higher densities in regions closer to zero, whereas for Duch adults this is more distributed across a greater range of emotion intensity scores.

Exploratory Analyses

Facial Expression Intensity Across Emotions, Age, and Country

In addition to our pre-registered analyses, we also sought to explore any differences in emotional expressivity across age and culture, when also considering specific emotions. To this end, we performed an additional beta linear mixed model, including age group, country, and emotion category (as well as their interactions) as fixed effects. The full regression output and analysis can be found in Supplementary Material 2. The model revealed a significant interaction effect between emotion category and age, as well as an interaction effect between emotion category and country. When zooming in on the emotion category by age contrasts, the results revealed that children displayed significantly more intense fear and happiness compared to adults. The emotion category by country contrasts revealed significant cultural differences across all emotion categories. Compared to the Netherlands, Japanese participants were more likely to show higher intensity sadness and fear expressions, and lower intensity disgust and happiness expressions. The full results of this model are presented in Figure S2 and Table S13.

Relationship Between Self-Reported and Expressed Emotions Across Emotion Categories, Age, and Country

Next, we aimed to quantify whether the relation between participants' self-reported emotion and corresponding facial expression varied across emotion categories, age groups, and countries. The details of the analysis can be found in Supplementary Materials 2.

Importantly, the analyses revealed a significant self-report score × emotion category × country interaction effect, such that, in the Netherlands, both children and adults displayed more intense facial expressions of happiness as their self-reported happiness increased, compared to Japanese children and adults. In Japan, higher self-reported happiness was associated with more intense expressions of happiness for children only, whereas for adults this relation was non-significant. In addition, for Dutch adults, higher self-reported sadness was associated with more intense corresponding facial expressions of sadness, though the equivalent relation for fear was non-significant. Japanese children additionally showed a positive association between self-reported and expressed disgust. Interestingly, while Japanese children and adults generally displayed high levels of sadness, this was not related to their self-report scores (Figure 3).

EMOTIONS ACROSS CULTURE AND DEVELOPMENT

The relationship between self-reported emotion and facial expressions was non-significant across all other combinations of emotion, age group and country (Table S14). These findings indicate that Dutch adults' experiences of sadness and happiness (but not fear or disgust) were informative of their corresponding facial expressions, but this was not the case for Japanese adults for any emotion assessed. Dutch and Japanese children showed a broadly similar pattern for happiness, with self-reported happiness predictive of facial expressions of happiness in both groups; Japanese children additionally showed this correspondence for disgust. Intensity, Split Across Age Group and Country, for Each Emotion Category Separately

Participant Exclusions

We screened all participants' response data for evidence of inattentive or invalid responding prior to analysis. Participants were excluded if they gave identical (or near identical, e.g., alternating only between two adjacent values) responses across all trials, such as ratings of 0 or 100 in every item on every video. This resulted in the exclusion of n = 10 participants, all of whom were Dutch children. Note that screening was not conducted blind to participant nationality; however, the exclusion criterion (identical or near-identical responses across all trials) was applied uniformly and did not involve subjective judgment.

Sampling Plan

Since we used Bayesian methods of statistical inference for our emotion perception analyses, we pre-registered a stopping rule of collecting data until we reached strong evidence (BF > 10) for either the alternative or null hypothesis of primary interest -namely, a three-way interaction between expresser country, observer country, and observer age group (reflecting an in-group advantage moderated by age), which in turn required comparable evidence for the underlying two-way interaction between expresser and observer country. We originally pre-registered a target of n = 200 per group (N = 800 total). Due to resource constraints, particularly in recruiting child participants, we did not reach this target in both child groups (n = 52 Japanese children; n = 105 Dutch children; see Table 5 for full sample characteristics). Because Bayes factors can be interpreted at any sample size without requiring a fixed pre-specified sample size, we were still able to draw valid conclusions about the strength of evidence given the data collected, even though the target evidential threshold may not have been reached in the child groups.

Design

This study had a factorial design with two between-subjects' factors: age of the observer (2 levels: adults, children), country of the observer (2 levels: Netherlands, Japan) and three within-subjects' factors: age of the expresser (2 levels: adults vs. children), country of the expresser (2 levels: Netherlands, Japan), and target emotion category of the expresser (4 levels: happiness, sadness, disgust and fear), the last being only of exploratory interest. As indicated, we examined the effects of these variables on two separate agreement indices: the absolute distance between observers' ratings and expressers' self-reported emotion, and the absolute distance between observers' ratings and facial expression intensity, as computed by the software FaceReader (Noldus, Wageningen).

Procedure

In this study, we asked an independent group of same-age observers as the participants in Study 1 to view the processed video stimuli (see processing details below in "Materials") and rate these according to which emotion(s) they believed the Study 1 participant (i.e., the expresser) experienced. We indicated that children could complete the task in the presence of their parents, but that parents should not interfere or help their children in any way. After reading the information about the task (or in the case of children, watching an instruction video), providing consent, and filling in some demographic information, participants were shown a subset of n = 16 stimuli from Study 1 to rate in randomized order.

These stimuli were fully balanced for culture, emotion and age, such that each participant saw one child and one adult from each culture for each of the four emotion categories.

Participants were free to re-watch all videos as many times as they saw fit. Participants used the same rating system as was used in Study 1: a series of sliding scales with a list of emotion words presented in their native language, (e.g., "The person in this video clip feels happy/sad/fear/disgust/neutral [1-100]"). Additionally, they were asked to indicate the expresser's valence and arousal levels on the same scale as Study 1. After participants rated all stimuli, they were provided with a plain-language debriefing with information about the task and our aims. The experiment took approximately 25 minutes for children, and 15 minutes for adults.

Materials

We only used the 20-second trimmed videos from Study 1 for which we had obtained consent from participants (and in the case of children, their parents). We defined a-priori a series of eligibility criteria. To achieve a fully balanced design, we required a pool of n = 32 unique videos per emotion category, split evenly across both countries and age groups (total = 128 unique stimuli). All videos in which the self-reported experience of the target emotion was higher than 10 for the target emotion were considered eligible for inclusion. Using a series of independent samples t-tests, it was confirmed that there were also no significant differences in self-report scores between countries on each emotion category, for each age group separately (all p's > .05). We assessed videos chronologically according to the date that Study 1 participants came to the lab, up until we reached the total maximum number of stimuli needed. The emotion perception experiment itself was conducted entirely online. We presented video stimuli using Qualtrics, and participants completed this task using a laptop on a web browser.

Analysis Pipeline

Calculation of Emotion Perception Agreement

EMOTIONS ACROSS CULTURE AND DEVELOPMENT

We operationalized emotion perception agreement by examining the absolute distance between: a) self-and observer-reported emotional experience and b) facial expression intensity (as derived by FaceReader) and observer-reported emotion scores on the target emotion specifically. For example, if a stimulus presented to an expresser in Study 1 was intended to induce the emotion "happiness", we calculated a self-and observer-reported emotion agreement score by comparing both values on the "happiness" scale alone (not considering the values on other emotion scales). The same premise applied for calculation of the agreement scores between observer-reports and facial expression intensity scores. For facial expression analyses, we took the peak intensity score of each emotion as calculated by

FaceReader during the 20-second recording and multiplied this by 100. This gave a rating of the intensity of each expressed emotion on the same scale as the observer-reported scores (0-100).

Statistical Models

We implemented all models using the brms package in R Studio unless otherwise specified. Since agreement scores were bounded (values could not be higher than 100 or less than 0), first transformed the data according to the recommendations of Smithson and Verkuilen (2006), in the same way as Study 1, which resulted in a dependent variable that included no zeros or ones. Then, using sum-to-zero coding, we fit two Bayesian regression models, one model for each outcome: absolute distance between: a) self-and observerreported emotional experience and b) facial expression intensity (as derived by FaceReader) and observer-reported emotion scores on the target emotion specifically.

These models used Beta error distributions that predicted agreement by observer age, observer country, expresser age, expresser country. In addition to these main effects, we included an additional three-way (observer age * observer country * expresser country) interaction term to test our hypothesis regarding the influence of both culture and age on emotion recognition. In an additional series of exploratory models, we re-ran our main models but included the effect of emotion category as an additional interaction term to delineate whether the effects in our preregistered analyses held when considering the potentially influential effect of emotion category.

In all models, we included random intercepts for each observer (nested in age category) and expresser ID (to account for potential differences in the ease in which observers could judge specific expressers). We specified Gaussian priors for all fixed effects.

In all cases, for the intercept, we specified a weakly informative prior with M = 0 and SD = 5.

For all other fixed effects, we specify a conservative prior with M = 0 and SD = 1, placing most probability mass on small effects. For all variance parameters, we retain default priors.

To inspect model fit, we examined Rhat and ESS values, as well as by visual inspection of the trace diagnostics and posterior predictive check plots. We report coefficients (b) on the logit scale alongside exponentiated coefficients, exp(b), to facilitate interpretation.

Exponentiated main-effect coefficients represent odds ratios, whereas exponentiated interaction coefficients represent ratios of odds ratios.

Sensitivity Analyses

To examine the robustness of our findings, we performed a sensitivity analysis on all our models by adjusting our priors and examining whether the interpretation of our results changed. We performed three separate analyses -each containing either a narrow, wider, or widest prior and inspected each outcome to determine whether the adjustment of the priors had putative impact on the interpretation of our findings. Additionally, posterior predictive checks indicated inadequate fit of the preregistered observer-self-report discrepancy model, with the model showed higher density near zero than one than in the observed data. We therefore fitted a zero-one-inflated beta sensitivity model to accommodate exact zeros and ones without boundary correction. Predictive fit improved, although some small discrepancies remained.

EMOTIONS ACROSS CULTURE AND DEVELOPMENT

The results of this analysis are presented in Supplementary Materials 3 and did not indicate major effects of prior specification on the interpretation of our findings.

Results

Correspondence Between Self-Reported and Observer-Reported Emotions Across Age and Cultural Groups

In the first pre-registered analysis, we examined the correspondence between observers' ratings of expressers' emotions and expressers' self-reported emotional experiences. We modelled the absolute distance between self-reported and observer-reported emotion scores, such that lower values indicated closer correspondence and higher values indicated greater discrepancy (see Table 6 for overview of these scores collapsed across participant groups). To this end, we conducted a Bayesian beta mixed effects model which tested the effects of age group, country of the observer, and the country of the expresser on the absolute agreement between the self-and observer-reported emotion scores. The model, displayed in Table 7, revealed a credible effect of expresser country and observer country.

This effect was such that, across all observer groups, observers' emotion ratings were more The model revealed no other interaction effects (all 95% CIs spanned zero). Most critically, we found no evidence for a cultural in-group advantage on emotion perception, supported by examination of the Bayes factors for our competing hypotheses. The first, which posited an effect of culture in the absence of an effect of age (i.e., an observer × expresser country interaction), revealed very strong evidence for the absence of an effect BF01 = 48.26. The second, which posited an effect of culture moderated by age (i.e., an observer country × expresser country × observer age interaction), revealed similarly very strong evidence for the absence of an effect BF01 = 65.1. Note sum-to-zero contrasts used.

EMOTIONS ACROSS CULTURE AND DEVELOPMENT

Correspondence Between Facial Expression Intensity Scores and Observer-Reported Emotions Across Age and Cultural Groups

In the second pre-registered analysis, we examined the correspondence between observers' emotion ratings and observed facial expression intensity for the target emotion. As in the preceding analysis, we modelled the absolute difference between the two measures, such that lower values indicated closer correspondence and higher values indicated greater discrepancy. We fitted a Bayesian beta mixed-effects model with the same fixed-effects structure as in the self-report analysis. The model, displayed in Table 8, similarly revealed a main effect of expresser country, b = -0.15, 95% CI = [-0.30, -0.00], exp(b) = 0.86, but in the opposite direction. Across observer groups, the difference between observers' emotion ratings and FaceReader target-emotion intensity scores was larger for Dutch than Japanese expressers. In other words, observers' ratings corresponded more closely with the emotion intensity observable in Japanese compared to Dutch facial expressions. Examination of the key interaction effects of interest revealed that this was independent of the age and cultural group of the observer. Regarding the two-way (observer × expresser culture) interaction, that could reveal an ingroup advantage, the Bayes factor revealed very strong evidence for the absence of an effect, BF01 = 66.84. Furthermore, regarding the three-way (observer country × expresser country × observer age) interaction, the Bayes factor also revealed very strong for the absence of an effect, BF10 = 73.4. Therefore, we found evidence of no in-group advantage in how emotions were judged relative to their facial expression intensity.

Taken together, observers' ratings aligned less closely with Japanese expressers' selfreported emotions, but more closely with the emotion intensity observable in Japanese facial

EMOTIONS ACROSS CULTURE AND DEVELOPMENT expressions. Neither pattern varied by observers' cultural background or age group, providing evidence no cultural in-group advantage on emotion perception. Bold rows reflect statistically meaningful effects. Sum-to-zero contrasts used.

Taken together, although these analyses identified a small number of emotion-specific patterns -and very few patterns additionally qualified by observer country and age -these effects generally did not suggest evidence of an in-group advantage in emotion perception overall.

General Discussion

There has been much debate in the literature regarding the extent to which expressions of emotion are shared across cultures. However, this research has been limited by a primary focus on adult emotion perception, the use of posed stimuli, and little consideration of people's experience of emotions. Across two preregistered studies, we addressed these limitations and examined the experience, expression, and perception of happiness, sadness, fear, and disgust among children and adults in Japan and the Netherlands. In Study 1, we found that self-reported emotional experiences were broadly similar across countries, whereas Dutch expressers displayed more intense facial expressions that more closely matched their own subjectively reported feelings than Japanese expressers. In Study 2, observers' ratings across cultures corresponded less closely with Japanese than Dutch expressers' self-reported emotions, but more closely with Japanese than Dutch expressers' facial-expression intensity. Neither pattern varied by observers' country, providing evidence for a lack of cultural in-group advantage.

Emotion Experience, Expression, and Perception Across Age and Country

Regarding the relation between emotional experience and expression, the cultural difference in facial-expression intensity is notable because it emerged despite broadly comparable self-reported emotional experiences across countries. The finding that Dutch participants generally displayed higher intensity facial expressions compared to Japanese participants is in line with some previous studies that found that Japanese (and other East Asian) participants typically display lower intensity facial expression compared to Western participants (e.g., Cowen et al., 2024; Schouten et al., 2020). We further extend this body of work through our inclusion of a developmental sample. Our analyses revealed that significant differences in expression intensity between Dutch and Japanese participants was mainly driven by differences between Dutch and Japanese adults' displayed facial expression intensity, while we found no differences in facial emotion intensity between children in the Netherlands and Japan. This may suggest that Japanese children, unlike Japanese adults, may not have fully internalized the display rules for emotions in their culture, which dictate generally low expressivity of emotions (Ekman et al., 1969; Matsumoto et al., 2008; Schouten et al., 2020) and expressed emotions with similar intensity as Dutch children. An additional interesting finding regarding cultural differences was that the associations between self-reported experience and visible facial emotional expression intensity was generally weaker for Japanese adults. This implies that these participants not only show lower intensity emotional expressions, but also that these expressions were less reflective of their internal states. This is perhaps also attributable to the display rules that more strongly regulate emotional expressions in Eastern Asian cultures (Safdar et al., 2009; Song et al., 2024).

It is perhaps no surprise then that, in Study 2, observers' ratings corresponded less closely with Japanese than Dutch expressers' self-reported emotions. However, conversely, observers' ratings corresponded more closely with the facial-expression intensity of Japanese than Dutch expressers. This implies that observers could better judge what Dutch participants felt based on their displayed emotions in the videos, likely because Dutch participants' selfreported feelings were more often associated with their displayed facial expression intensity.

For Dutch expressers, the face seemed to provide a relatively more informative cue to selfreported emotional experience. For Japanese expressers, by contrast, observers' ratings corresponded more closely to facial-expression intensity but less closely to self-reported experience. Thus, Japanese facial behaviour may have provided a relatively consistent cue to the emotion visibly expressed, while serving a less direct cue to expressers' reported inner experiences.

While patterns across Study 2 depended on the expresser's country, there was no effect of the observers' country, providing evidence for a lack of cultural in-group advantage in emotion perception. This result may sound surprising given a previous meta-analysis which found evidence for this (Elfenbein & Ambady, 2002). However, a more recent study by Cong and colleagues (2025b) challenged these findings, suggesting that when balanced designs are used (in which observers of both countries judge expressers of both countries) these effects may disappear.

Our study, which similarly used a balanced design, is consistent with this more recent study. Together, the findings of the two studies suggest that similar emotional experiences across cultures may be accompanied by differences in the intensity of facial emotional expressions, particularly among adults, with consequences for how closely others can infer emotions from the face.

Limitations and Future Directions

There are a few limitations in our design worth mentioning. Firstly, we provided participants with emotion labels when providing their self-reported emotional state and this constrained their responses to several emotions (e.g., happiness, sadness, fear, disgust), framing the emotion space as containing discrete categories. As such, future research may consider using experience sampling or free-response questions to allow participants to indicate their emotional state in their own words. Another key limitation of our study was that we were unable to adequately induce self-reported fear in our child sample in Study 1.

However, we observed prototypical fear facial expressions in children, that were significantly more intense than those of adults. This could suggest that children may not have wanted to report feeling afraid, even if they did so, given the negative associations with this emotion state at this age (Dadds et al., 1998). Yet, we should be careful when drawing conclusions about this emotion in children specifically. Future studies could consider the use of physiological recordings (e.g., heart rate, electrodermal activity) to better characterize the participants' emotional responding and to better tease apart where any differences in emotional responding lie (Mauss et al., 2005). A final limitation concerns the Study 2 observer sample sizes. Owing to resource constraints, we did not reach the preregistered stopping rule of 200 participants in each child observer group. Although this shortfall does not invalidate the Bayesian interpretation of the primary analyses, it warrants caution when interpreting the results, and particularly the exploratory, emotion-specific findings.

Conclusion

Across two preregistered studies, we jointly examined emotional experience, facial expression, and emotion perception in Japanese and Dutch children and adults. Despite broadly similar self-reported emotional intensity across countries, Japanese participants displayed less intense facial expressions than Dutch participants, with cultural differences most pronounced among adults. Observers from both countries showed closer agreement with Dutch expressers' reported emotional experiences, but closer agreement with Japanese expressers' facial-expression intensity. Neither pattern depended on observer country, providing no evidence for a cultural in-group advantage. By linking expression production with perception and subjective feelings, our findings suggest that cultural differences in emotion involve not only how strongly feelings are expressed in the face, but also how closely observers' judgements correspond to those feelings and facial expressions. This highlights the need for psychological theories of emotion and social understanding to account for culturally variable associations among emotion experience, expression, and perception.

Participants

This research project was approved by the local Research Ethics Committee at Leiden University (#5086) and the local Research Ethics Committee and Tokyo Woman's Christian University (#A2024-4). A total of N = 552 participants were recruited online via social media, the university research participation platform at Leiden and Tokyo Woman's Christian University, as well as in local schools. Children were required to be between the ages of 8 and 12-years-old, and adults between 18-40-years-old. A breakdown of participant demographic information is displayed in Table 5. In addition to age requirements, we required participants to be fluent in Dutch (for the Dutch wing of the study) and Japanese (for the Japanese wing of the study). Finally, since we used visual stimuli, all participants were required to have normal or corrected-to-normal vision. In Japan, 99% of adults and 100% of children's parents identified as Japanese. In the Netherlands, on the advice of the ethical review board, we asked adult participants whether they identified as coming from a Western or non-Western background. Of our Dutch participants, 94% of adults identified as Western.

Collecting demographic information from Dutch children (or their parents) proved difficult, and, as such, we did not collect this data.

Participants were reimbursed according to the standard rate of the local ethics committee, which differed across sites. Dutch children were entered into a raffle to win one of 25 small toy prizes (value approximately €10). Dutch adults were reimbursed according to the standard rate at Leiden University: research credits or €4,25. The parents of Japanese children received a 1500¥ gift card for their child's participation, while Japanese adults received a 600¥ gift card.

Effects of Emotion Category on Correspondence Across Age and Culture

As in Study 1, as an additional exploratory analysis, we examined whether correspondence between observer ratings and the comparison measures differed across emotion categories. We fitted Bayesian beta mixed-effects models that extended the preregistered models by including emotion category and its interactions with observer age group, observer country, and expresser country. Detailed model output and estimated marginal contrasts are reported in Supplementary Materials 3 (Tables S1, S2, and S3).

Because both outcomes indexed absolute differences, we describe the findings in terms of closer or poorer correspondence.

Observers' ratings matched Japanese expressers' self-reported emotions less closely than Dutch expressers' self-reported emotions for fear, among both child and adult observers.

Among adults, the same pattern emerged for disgust and sadness. The disgust and sadness patterns, however, were qualified by observer country: the poorer correspondence with Japanese expressers' self-reports was most apparent among Dutch adult observers for disgust, but among Japanese adult observers for sadness.

When observer ratings were compared with the emotion intensity observable in facial expressions, the overall pattern was reversed. For disgust and happiness, both child and adult observers' ratings corresponded more closely with the emotion intensity observable in Japanese than Dutch facial expressions. Adult observers also showed this pattern for fear. These effects were broadly similar across observer countries, although the stronger correspondence between observer ratings and Japanese facial-expression intensity for happiness was especially pronounced among Japanese observers.

These inconsistent findings leave open not only whether an in-group advantage emerges during development, but also what such an advantage would represent. Previous attempts cannot distinguish whether cross-cultural differences in apparent recognition perception arise from differences in expressers' emotional experiences, their facial expressions, observers' interpretations, or a combination of these factors. Addressing this issue requires studies that jointly assess elicited expressions, expressers' reported experiences, and observers' judgements in children and adults from different cultural contexts.
